title: Grace Hopper: The Moth in the Relay and the First Compiler
source_book: The Education of a Computer (Proceedings of the ACM)
source_chapter: ACM '52: Proceedings of the 1952 ACM National Meeting, pp. 243–249
source_edition: Association for Computing Machinery, New York
authenticity_note: Based on Grace Hopper's September 9, 1947 Harvard Mark II logbook entry pasting a real moth ('First actual case of bug being found') and her pioneering 1952 invention of the A-0 compiler translating English words into machine code.
summary: Pioneering computer scientist and US Navy Rear Admiral Grace Hopper removed an actual moth trapped inside Relay #70 of the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947, coining 'debugging'. In 1952, she invented the world's first compiler—insisting that humans should program computers in plain English words rather than obscure binary numbers.
content:
In the 1940s and 50s, programming a computer was a mind-numbing ordeal. Programmers had to write endless strings of octal or binary numbers—0s and 1s—directly into the hardware. If a programmer made a single typo, the entire sequence collapsed.

U.S. Navy lieutenant and Yale mathematics Ph.D. Grace Hopper was stationed at Harvard University working on the colossal electromechanical Mark II computer. On a muggy September afternoon in 1947, the machine suddenly conked out.

Hopper and her team checked the endless rows of mechanical relays. Deep inside Relay #70 in Panel F, they found a live moth trapped between the electrical contact points, beating its wings and shorting out the circuit! Hopper carefully extracted the insect with tweezers and taped it into the official logbook with the notation: *"First actual case of bug being found."* While the word 'bug' had older engineering roots, Hopper's wit permanently popularized 'bug' and 'debugging' in the computing lexicon.

Hopper had a much greater vision: *"Why must humans learn the machine's tedious language? Why can't the computer be taught to understand human English?"*

Senior scientists scoffed, telling her: *"Computers can only do arithmetic! They cannot understand words!"*

Refusing to listen, in 1952 Hopper wrote the world's first **compiler**, the **A-0 System**. A compiler is a master program that reads human-readable words—like `ADD`, `SUBTRACT`, `MULTIPLY`—and automatically translates them into the machine's native binary code.

Hopper went on to help develop **COBOL** (Common Business-Oriented Language), which enabled people with no engineering degrees to write computer programs. Today, every high-level language—from Python and C++ to JavaScript—traces its lineage directly to Grace Hopper's stubborn belief that human language belongs in computing.

The process of identifying and removing errors or bugs from computer hardware or software.
A computer programming language consisting of binary or hexadecimal instructions which a computer can respond to directly.
